section_summary: This section continues a Spanish-language economic monograph examining the Great Depression, Japan’s export expansion, trade barriers, import and export quotas, and the most-favored-nation clause. It then applies that framework to Peru, contrasting trade with Japan and Great Britain and documenting the effect of Japanese cotton textiles on Peruvian mills. The closing pages describe Peru’s treaty, tariff, and quota responses and begin reviewing quota arrangements with France, Spain, and Chile.

subfiles.title: Economic study of trade quotas, the most-favored-nation clause, and Japanese cotton competition in Peru (continuation)
subfiles.about: A wide-ranging study of quota systems and their use to protect Peru’s cotton-textile industry against rapidly expanding Japanese imports.
subfiles.summary: The continuation first attributes contemporary trade restrictions to the Depression, industrial protection, Japanese export organization, low wages, and yen depreciation. It classifies trade barriers and surveys export and import quotas, including the Chadbourne sugar plan and quota practices across Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and colonial territories, before considering their compatibility with the most-favored-nation clause. The Peruvian portion uses financial, production, employment, and foreign-trade data to contrast the country’s adverse balance with Japan and favorable commercial relationship with Great Britain. It then traces the surge of Japanese cotton goods, the resulting pressure on Peruvian factories, and government responses including denunciation of the Japanese commercial treaty, higher tariffs, the import-quota decree of 10 May 1935, and negotiations with France, Spain, and Chile.
